la:adj:alacrior.gloss: lively; brisk; quick; eager; active; peppy; excited
senses: comparative degree of alacer
cheerfulness, liveliness, gaiety, animation
alacrity, eagerness, persistence, zeal, fervour, ardour
joy, rejoicing, exultation, triumph
la:noun:alacritas.html:
ălăcrĭtas, ātis, f.
alacer
,
the condition or quality of alacer, liveliness, ardor, briskness, alacrity, eagerness, promptness, joy, gladness: alacritas rei publicae defendendae,: mirā sum alacritate ad litigandum,; so : alacritas studiumque pugnandi,: animi incitatio atque alacritas,: alacritas animae suae,: finem orationis ingens alacritas consecuta est,: (naves) citae remis augebantur alacritate militum in speciem ac terrorem,.—Of animals: canum in venando,. —Of a joyous state of mind as made known by external demeanor, transport, rapture, ecstasy: inanis alacritas, id est laetitia gestiens,: vir temperatus, constans, sine metu, sine aegritudine, sine alacritate ullā, sine libidine,. —With obj. gen., joy on account of something: clamor Romanorum alacritate perfecti operis sublatus,—* In plur.: vigores quidam mentium et alacritates,.

la:noun:alauda.gloss: a lark; the crested lark, the skylark
senses: a lark; the crested lark, the skylark
la:noun:alauda.html:
ălauda, ae, f.
Celtic; lit. great songstress, from al, high, great, and aud, song; cf. the Fr. alouette; Breton. al' choueder; v. Diefenbach in Zeitschriften für vergl. Sprachf. IV. p. 391
.
The lark, .—
ălauda, the name of a legion raised by Cœsar, in Gaul, at his own expense (prob. so called from the decoration of their helmet): unam (legionem) ex Transalpinis conscriptam, vocabulo quoque Gallico (Alauda enim appellabatur) civitate donavit,: cum legione Alaudarum ad urbem pergit,: Huc accedunt Alaudae ceterique veterani,.

la:adj:alacer.gloss: lively; brisk; quick; eager; active; peppy; excited
senses: lively; brisk; quick; eager; active; peppy; excited
glad; happy; cheerful
la:adj:alacer.html:
ălăcer, cris, e, adj. (also in
masc. alacris, Enn., v. below; , and ; cf. P.—In more ancient times, alacer comm.; cf. , and 2. acer) [perh. akin to alere = to nourish, and olēre = to grow; cf. ; Auct. ad ], lively, brisk, quick, eager, active; glad, happy, cheerful (opp. languidus; cf. Doed. Syn. 3, 247, and 4, 450.—In the class. per., esp. in Cicero, with the access. idea of joyous activity).
Lit.
Of men: ignotus juvenum coetus, alternā vice Inibat alacris, Bacchio insultans modo, Enn. ap. P.: quid tu es tristis? quidve es alacris?why are you so disturbed? or why so excited? ( = incitatus, commotus, Ruhnk.): videbant Catilinam alacrem atque laetum,active and joyous,: valentes imbecillum, alacres perterritum superare,: Aman laetus et alacer,: alacres animo sumus,are eager in mind, Manut.; —With ad: alacriores ad reliquum perficiendum, Auct. ad : ad maleficia,: ad bella suscipienda alacer et promptus animus,; so : ad rem gerendam,.—With super: alacri corde super omnibus,.—In Sall. once for nimble, active: cum alacribus saltu, cum velocibus cursu certabat, Fragm. 62, p. 248 Gerl.—
Of animals: equus,: bestiae, Auct. ad . —
Transf., poet., of concrete and abstract things: alacris voluptas,a lively pleasure,; so, alacres enses, quick, ready to cut, : involant (in pugnam) impetu alacri,with a spirited, vigorous onset,. —Sup. not used; cf. P.; Rudd. I. p. 177, n. 48.—Adv.: ălăcrĭter, briskly, eagerly, .—Comp., .

senses: to go

la:noun:ala.gloss: a wing (appendage of an animal's body that enables it to fly)
senses: a wing (appendage of an animal's body that enables it to fly)
the armpit (the upper and under part of the arm, where it unites with the shoulder)
shoulder blade, axilla (the hollow where the foreleg is joined to the shoulder)
the hollow where a limb joins the trunk of a tree
wings, side halls or porches, waiting areas, colonnades, side apartments (side rooms off the main room, the side apartments on the right and left of a court)
a wing (portion of an army, cavalry force (usually) deployed on an army's flank)
wings (the members of a group placed along the perimeter)
la:noun:ala.html:
āla, ae, f.
for axla, contr. from axilla, ; cf. ἄγχος = ὦμος (Hesych.) = shoulder = O. H. Germ. Ahsala; Germ. Achsel
.
Lit., a wing, as of a bird: galli plausu premunt alas, Enn. ap. ; : Me. Vox mihi ad aurīs advolavit. So. Ne ego homo infelix fui, qui non alas intervelli, that I did not pluck off its wings, .—Poet., of the gods: Mors atris circumvolat alis,: volucris Fati Tardavit alas,: bibulae Cupidinis alae,: furvis circumdatus alis Somnus,: me jocundis Sopor impulit alis,: Madidis Notus evolat alis,.—Of sails: velorum pandimus alas,.—Of oars: classis centenis remiget alis,: remigium alarum, (cf. Hom. Od. 11, 125); so inversely remi is used of wings: super fluctus alarum insistere remis, (cf. πτεροῖς ἐρέσσει, Eur. Iphig. Taur. 289; Aeschyl. Agam. 52; and cf. ). —Of wind and lightning: Nisus Emicat et ventis et fulminis ocior alis,—
Transf.
In man, the upper and under part of the arm, where it unites with the shoulder; the armpit, ; : aliquid sub alā portare,: hirquinae,: hirsutae,: halitus oris et alarum vitia,: virus alarum et sudores,: sudor alarum, (many Romans were accustomed to pluck out the hair from the armpits, ; ; v. alipilus).—
In animals, the hollow where the foreleg is joined to the shoulder; the shoulder - blade.—Of elephants, .—Of frogs, .—
In trees and plants, the hollow where the branch unites with the stem, ; so ; —
In buildings, the wings, the side apartments on the right and left of the court, the side halls or porches, the colonnades; called also in Gr. πτερά, ; .—
In milit. lang., the wing of an army (thus conceived of as a bird of prey), commonly composed of the Roman cavalry and the troops of the allies, esp. their horsemen; hence, alarii in contrast with legionarii, and separated from them in enumeration, also having a leader, called praefectus alae, ; cf. Lips. de Milit. Rom. 1, 10 Manut.; ; Herz. ad ; Smith, Dict. Antiq.; Cincius ap. ; cf. : Alae, equites: ob hoc alae dicti, quia pedites tegunt alarum vice,: peditatu, equitibus atque alis cum hostium legionibus pugnavit, Cato ap. ; : dextera ala (in alas divisum socialem exercitum habebat) in primā acie locata est,; —An ala, as a military division, usu. consisted of about 500 men, .!*? Such alae gave names to several towns, since they were either levied from them, quartered in them, or, after the expiration of their time of service, received the lands of such towns.—So, Ala Flaviana, Ala Nova, et saep. (cf. castrum, II. 1. fin.).

senses: having wings, winged
la:adj:alatus.html:
ālātus, a, um, adj.
ala
,
furnished with wings, winged (only poet.).—Of Mercury: plantae, * : pes,: Phoebus alatis aethera carpit equis,.

la:adv:alacriter.gloss: eagerly; joyfully; with relish or alacrity
senses: eagerly; joyfully; with relish or alacrity

la:noun:alapa.gloss: slap, smack (with the flat of the hand)
senses: slap, smack (with the flat of the hand)
la:noun:alapa.html:
ălăpa, ae, f.
akin to -cello, to smite, as if calapa; cf. κόλαφος
,
a stroke or blow upon the cheek with the open hand, a box on the ear: ducere gravem alapam alicui,to give,: ministri eum alipis caedebant,; ; ; esp. among actors, for the purpose of exciting a laugh among their auditors, * ; * .—When a slave was emancipated, his master gave him an alapa; hence, poet.: multo majoris alapae mecum veneunt,i. e. with me freedom is much more dearly purchased,.

la:adj:alarius.gloss: Of or pertaining to the wings of an army, that is upon the wing.
senses: Of or pertaining to the wings of an army, that is upon the wing.
la:adj:alarius.html:
ālārĭus, a, um (less freq. ālāris, e), adj.
ala

that is upon the wing (of an army), of the wing (opp. legionarii, v. ala, II.
